status_summary: No broad revision of the rating schedule aimed at savings for future claimants was found. The nearest action was a VA interim final rule, published and effective 2026-02-17, amending 38 CFR 4.10 so conditions are rated at their medicated level; VA said it responded to the Court of Appeals for Veterans Claims decision in Ingram v. Collins (2025), which it said could require readjudicating over 350,000 pending claims, and OIRA treated the rule as economically significant and deregulatory. It did not distinguish future from existing claimants and gave no dollar estimate, though a letter from congressional Democrats of 2026-02-24 cites an estimated $23 billion in cost savings without naming who produced it. Secretary Collins halted enforcement on 2026-02-19 and VA rescinded the rule on 2026-02-27, restoring the prior text without announcing a re-proposal, after opposing comments (more than 18,000 per the Senate committee minority page, nearly 20,000 per Military Times) and objections from lawmakers and veterans groups; VA's rescission notice describes the rule as a clarification of existing policy during an ongoing court action. Condition-specific rating proposals since 2025 (painful scars, endometriosis, bradycardia) are narrow, and two of the three ease access or set a rating floor.

timeline.event: VA proposes adding a note to diagnostic code 7804 (painful scars) stating that objective evidence of pain is required, which the proposal says matches current policy; the abstract describes it as a clarification, not a change in rating levels.
VA proposes removing the laparoscopy confirmation requirement for establishing service connection for endometriosis (diagnostic code 7629), which would make service connection easier to establish.
VA proposes a minimum 10 percent evaluation for bradycardia once a pacemaker is implanted, aligning diagnostic code 7009 with code 7018.

VA publishes an interim final rule, Evaluative Rating: Impact of Medication (91 FR 7118), effective immediately. It adds language to 38 CFR 4.10 barring examiners from estimating or discounting improvement from medication or treatment, citing Ingram v. Collins; OIRA designated it economically significant, a major rule and deregulatory under EO 14192.

Secretary Collins announces the rule will not be enforced; Senator Blumenthal, the Senate Veterans' Affairs ranking member, welcomes the halt and says the rule must be permanently withdrawn. Military Times reports that twenty lawmakers wrote to VA asking for revocation and that at least one lawsuit was filed (no lawsuit docket was read).

Senate Veterans' Affairs Ranking Member Blumenthal and House Veterans' Affairs Ranking Member Takano, joined by nine other senators and eleven other representatives, send Secretary Collins a letter asking VA to fully and permanently rescind the interim final rule (still in the Code of Federal Regulations although enforcement was paused) and to answer questions by 2026-03-02 on the rule's legal justification, the number of veterans affected, and VA's planned action on its appeal of Ingram v. Collins. The committee page reports more than 18,000 public comments opposed the rule and the letter cites an estimated $23 billion in cost savings without saying who produced the estimate.

VA publishes a rescission of the interim final rule, effective immediately, restoring the prior text of 38 CFR 4.10. VA says it issued the rule to clarify existing policy and protect veterans' benefits during an ongoing court action, that many commenters read the rule as potentially harmful, that keeping it during a lengthy rulemaking could erode confidence, and that the rescission does not resolve the legal questions before the courts; it makes no commitment to a new rule or proposal.

Senator Blumenthal introduces S. 4140, the Carlton H. Ingram Veterans' Benefits Protection Act (cosponsors Duckworth, King, Murray, Gallego, Sanders, Baldwin; referred to the Veterans' Affairs Committee), which would amend 38 U.S.C. 1155 to require the rating schedule to discount the beneficial effects of medication or treatment where evidence can establish a baseline without them, codifying the Ingram standard. A bill tracker reports a hearing on 2026-04-29 and no passage in either chamber (tracker only; congress.gov was not read).

title: Revise the VA disability rating schedule to cut costs for future claimants
uncertainties: Classification is a judgment call. The Mandate objective is a broad, cost-motivated schedule revision for future claimants; the only cost-relevant rule found was framed by VA as a response to the Ingram decision, applied to all claims, and was withdrawn by VA itself rather than enjoined, so 'not_started' with the rule as context is a defensible alternative to 'blocked'. The $23 billion figure appears in the 2026-02-24 lawmakers' letter (its source is not stated) and in Military Times; it is not a VA figure, and neither the VA regulatory impact analysis nor the lawsuit was read. S. 4140's text was read at GovInfo; its 2026-04-29 hearing comes from a bill tracker (congress.gov was not fetched). A Federal Register API query of VA documents mentioning the rating schedule, run again in pass 5, found nothing after 2026-02-27; VA's Unified Agenda was still not read. VA's regulatory agenda was not found in Federal Register listings, so planned schedule rulemakings could exist that are not visible; a web search for post-March 2026 VASRD news returned only February 2026 coverage. The Mandate recommends OMB-cleared acceleration, and no source shows whether OMB reviewed the schedule beyond the OIRA designation of the interim rule.
